title: Caring for orphans
hookLine: two fingers held up, a little apart: that's how close the orphan's carer stands
tomorrow: can a weekly phone call count as a struggle?

lines: ONE IS HIM. WHO'S THE OTHER?
cards: Peace sign. Victory sign. Bunny ears behind a friend's head.
Two fingers up can mean a lot of things in a photo, and most of them are playful.
In one hadith, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ holds up two fingers, his pointing finger and his middle finger, with a little space between them, and the two fingers stand for two people. One of them is him.
Who is the other, standing that close?

teach.h: THE ORPHAN'S CARER, SIDE BY SIDE.
teach.b: The answer is in Sahih al-Bukhari: I and the one who looks after an orphan will be in Paradise like this. And he held up those two fingers, apart a little. That's the distance.
Not a row behind. Side by side. Here's why it lands: the Prophet grew up an orphan himself.

teach.h: DID HE NOT FIND THEE AN ORPHAN?
teach.b: The Qur'an says it to him directly, in Pickthall's words: "Did He not find thee an orphan and protect (thee)?" A few verses on comes what follows from it: "Therefore the orphan oppress not."
The one who was once the child without a father is told: now don't let that child be pushed around.

teach.h: KAFIL: THE ONE WHO HAS THEIR BACK.
teach.b: The hadith's word for the carer is kafil: the one who takes responsibility, who has a child's back over time.
So caring for an orphan isn't only one grand gesture. Some Muslims sponsor a child far away, and that counts.
So does the uncle who takes his brother's kids in, the neighbor who keeps showing up to the school play, the grandmother raising her grandson.
One thing worth telling a friend tonight: the man who promised that closeness had been that child first.
Two fingers, a small gap. Close enough to touch, and still two.

how: Muslims care for orphans by taking in relatives' children, sponsoring children through charities, and giving zakat and sadaqah toward their needs; many point to this hadith and the Prophet's own childhood when they do.

o: praying for children in a hospital ward
looking after a child who has lost a parent
a yearly gift to a children's charity fund

games.q: what's inside the teaching — tap the pairs.
p: found thee an orphan and protected

s: caring for an orphan in Islam just means sending money to a charity
sponsoring counts. but the hadith's word is kafil: the one who has a child's back over time.
the Qur'an says the Prophet was himself an orphan
93:6: did He not find thee an orphan and protect thee?
in the hadith, the orphan's carer ends up far from the Prophet, but still in Paradise
two fingers, apart a little. side by side.

games.q: your neighbor's teenage son lost his dad last year, and his mom works nights. you want to do something. what does the two-fingers hadith point to?
o: show up steadily: a ride, a meal, a seat at his games, week after week.
one big gift card for his mom, then give the family their privacy.
wait until he asks; looking after him is his own relatives' job.
games.why: the kafil is the one who takes on a child's care over time. steady and close: two fingers, a small gap.

practice: Hold up your pointing finger and middle finger, a small space between them, and look at how close they are. Breathing slowly, bring to mind one child you know who is carrying more than a child should.
Keep your fingers up as long as it's comfortable, then rest your hand.

wordCard.voice: Caring for orphans: taking responsibility for a child who has lost a parent. In the hadith, it puts the carer right beside the Prophet.

orig.note: Arabic: the one who looks after the orphan. kafil is someone who takes responsibility for another.

carryVoice: Keep this one: two fingers together, close enough to touch, and still two. Goodnight for now.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 5304 (also 6005): I and the one who looks after an orphan will be in Paradise like this, holding up his pointing and middle fingers, apart a little

sources.q: Did He not find thee an orphan and protect (thee)?
